newsitem.title: UK: ATHLETICS-SPACE-AGE CHRISTIE RULES OUT MAJOR RETURN.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-SPACE-AGE CHRISTIE RULES OUT MAJOR RETURN.

text.p: Linford Christie appeared dressed as a spaceman at a London nightclub on Friday but insisted he has completed his final mission as a major championship sprinter.
The former Olympic champion, now 36, was in typically spiky form as he helped launch his sponsors' new training shoe before flying to Australia on Monday for warm weather training and coaching.

He did not rule out trying to win a place in the British team at the European Cup in Munich in June, even though team coach Malcolm Arnold has indicated there are a number of promising younger candidates, but said he wanted to concentrate on helping other sprinters.

"I'm going to run for my club a lot, but no majors," said Christie. "I'm just having fun now. Athletics isn't my life. I've got other things. I've achieved all my goals and now I'm out there trying to help other athletes achieve theirs."

Christie's future plans, however, are rarely crystal clear and teasing an audience remains one of his favourite pastimes. "We're in January, the world championships are in August. I don't even think that far ahead."

His public relations advisors had promised that Christie would be providing "earthlings" with "information gleaned from alien life forms." As it turned out, those present at the 'Ministry of Sound' in Elephant and Castle, south London were merely shown his latest advertisement and given an opportunity to watch Christie act the role of a "nutty professor" in a hastily-erected laboratory on the dance-floor.
Dressed in an all-in-one skintight silver suit, Christie peered into one of the test tubes containing a cloudy liquid and said it reminded him of one of his urine samples.

Back in the real world, he declined to get too publicly involved in the current internal troubles facing the British Athletic Federation - "You're asking me to single-handedly solve the problems of the sport. I can't do that" - and said he had seen the recent story suggesting a faulty timing mechanism had led to him being disqualified for two false starts in the Olympic 100 metres final in Atlanta last year.

"You guys slated me for saying I felt I was hard done by. Some of the British press went as far as saying I did it on purpose. When an American comes out and says it, that's when you seem to want to believe. Believe what you want to believe."
